Daniel Sullivan directs with howling success.
What makes this production of 'Sylvia' such a treat is the inspired comic chemistry between Broderick and Ashford
Sylvia is a comedy as predictable as it is indestructible.
What a joy to see Ashford unleashed.
As long as we can sit back and laugh at Sylvia’s doggy antics while admiring Ashford’s comic flair, “Sylvia” is harmless fun.
So leave the deep-thinking cap at home, and settle in for some pleasurable laughs.

The play is an extended -- actually, an overextended -- Thurberesque cartoon about the competition between a man's dog and a man's wife. It is a romantic triangle for unrepentant animal people and the people who love them but just don't get it -- which, I guess, manages to include just about everyone.
The production is worth the trip for Ashford's antics alone.

Ashford gives a comic-genius performance, establishing herself as a full-fledged clown star, meaning she’s not only hilarious and eccentric but able to project both qualities, as well as an undertone of pathos, to the back of the house.
The gimmick of “Sylvia,” which is indeed a comedy — albeit a trifling one — resides in the casting of an actor as Sylvia.
And this contributes to the general feeling of weirdness inside the Cort Theatre.

Dog owners in the audience are identifiable by their guffaws over every recognizable mutt mannerism, but there’s enough meat here to sustain a half-hour playlet at best, in an overstretched conceit that runs an interminable two hours-plus.
This truly is one of those must-see performances that will stick with you for some time.
Daniel Sullivan's production of A.R. Gurney's 1995 play is so warm and bitingly funny, you'd have to be an absolute Grinch to resist its immense charms.
All in all, Sylvia is a delightfully benign canine-comedy.
Anyone looking for a solid example of that most endangered of species, the smart boulevard comedy, should consider adopting 'Sylvia' for an evening's entertainment.
Even the unenlightened -- that is, folks who don't already love dogs -- are bound to lose their hearts.

Ashford’s consistently hilarious, sometimes touching, always spot-on canine impersonation is the reason to see the first Broadway production of A.R. Gurney’s play about a man who falls in love with a stray dog that he finds in the park, endangering his marriage.
Unfortunately, she and Broderick lack chemistry and that is my only problem with an otherwise enjoyable and fun theatrical experience.
Sylvia is a fanciful but slight dessert sort of a play, so have yourself a satisfying meal before ordering it up.
This revival proves that some plays are every bit as timeless as man's best friend.
Fortunately, the verdict rests with the former.
Much of the play is fun but the march to the end falls rather flat.
There's a casting director out there who deserves a Milk-Bone. That reward is for realizing twinkly Annaleigh Ashford could so dynamically inhabit the title role in 'Sylvia'...
For the rest of us, 'Sylvia' ends up feeling like the proverbial dog that won't hunt.
All of this gimmickry — some of it written into the play, some of it resulting from Sullivan’s direction — wouldn’t matter if the characters, the dog included, weren’t so dull.
How can anyone not fall in love with Sylvia?
Ashford is incredibly talented.
If dogs could talk, Ashford would be barking up the right tree.
Bottom line: this is a very funny comedy and if you love dogs, you'll love 'Sylvia.'

"'Sylvia' is A.R. Gurney's most obvious (and probably only) crowd-pleaser...Whenever Ashford barks—'hey hey hey hey!'—it could be love, hate, anger, affection or irritation, and Ashford varies her tone and timbre to suit the occasion.

Twenty years after its debut at Manhattan Theatre Club, A.R. Gurney’s charming but inconsequential play has finally made it to Broadway. It presents the playwright in a much more favorable light than any of the three Gurney plays that Signature recently mounted.
The revival of “Sylvia,” its first on Broadway, is like a three-quarter carat diamond nested in Elizabeth Taylor’s engagement ring’s setting.
But the Broadway premiere of this boy-meets-girl (er, dog) story proves Gurney's 20-year-old trifle to be more table scraps than satisfying sit-down.
It's downright shameful when it happens at a $150-a-ticket Broadway play.
Ashford, dressed by costumer Ann Roth in a shaggy sweater and knee pads to protect her joints as she bounces around David Rockwell's perhaps too lovely set, is great at the job.
Considering Sylvia's wispy and dated plot, Mathew Broderick's low-energy performance, and Daniel Sullivan's flimsy direction, there is hardly any reason to sit up, pant or roll over with delight.

cn.t: Critics praise Annaleigh Ashford's delightful performance as the canine lead in Gurney's charming comedy, though some find the 1995 play lightweight and Broderick underwhelming. A warm crowd-pleaser for dog lovers that doesn't demand much depth.
